claim: The white-footed deermouse Peromyscus leucopus is a key reservoir in North America for agents of several zoonoses, including Lyme disease, babesiosis, anaplasmosis, and a viral encephalitis.
source: The white-footed deermouse Peromyscus leucopus, a long-lived rodent, is a key reservoir in North America for agents of several zoonoses, including Lyme disease, babesiosis, anaplasmosis, and a viral encephalitis.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the role of P. leucopus as a disease reservoir, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: P. leucopus remains persistently infected without apparent disability or diminished fitness.
source: While persistently infected, this deermouse is without apparent disability or diminished fitness.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing prior studies.

claim: LPS-treated P. leucopus displayed little transcription of interferon-gamma compared to mice and rats.
source: LPS-treated P. leucopus, in contrast to mice and rats, also displayed little transcription of interferon-gamma and lower magnitude fold-changes in type 1 interferon-stimulated genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript, including specific figures and tables showing Ifng transcription levels.

claim: LPS-treated P. leucopus showed lower magnitude fold-changes in type 1 interferon-stimulated genes compared to mice and rats.
source: LPS-treated P. leucopus, in contrast to mice and rats, also displayed little transcription of interferon-gamma and lower magnitude fold-changes in type 1 interferon-stimulated genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential expression of ISGs between species.

claim: Deermice were distinguished from mice and rats by LPS response profiles consistent with non-classical monocytes and alternatively-activated macrophages.
source: Deermice were distinguished from the mice and rats by LPS response profiles consistent with non-classical monocytes and alternatively-activated macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptional analysis data showing specific gene expression patterns (Nos2/Arg1, Akt1/Akt2, Cd14/Fcgr3 ratios).

claim: The phenomenon of reduced interferon response in P. leucopus was associated with comparatively reduced transcription of endogenous retrovirus sequences.
source: The phenomenon was associated with comparatively reduced transcription of endogenous retrovirus sequences and cytoplasmic pattern recognition receptors in the deermice.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing ERV transcription between species under LPS treatment.

claim: The phenomenon of reduced interferon response in P. leucopus was associated with comparatively reduced transcription of cytoplasmic pattern recognition receptors.
source: The phenomenon was associated with comparatively reduced transcription of endogenous retrovirus sequences and cytoplasmic pattern recognition receptors in the deermice.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing lower expression of PRRs like RIG-I in deermice.

claim: P. leucopus has a two-to-three fold longer life span than the house mouse, Mus musculus.
source: A related question—conceivably with the same answer—is what accounts for the two-to-three fold longer life span for P. leucopus than for the house mouse, Mus musculus (Labinskyy et al., 2009; Sacher and Hart, 1978) ?
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most deermice remain persistently infected but display scant inflammation in affected tissues.
source: Most deermice remain persistently infected but display scant inflammation in affected tissues (Cook and Barbour, 2015; Long et al., 2019; Moody et al., 1994), and without apparent consequence for fitness (Schwanz et al., 2011; Voordouw et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: Persistent infection in deermice occurs without apparent consequence for fitness.
source: Most deermice remain persistently infected but display scant inflammation in affected tissues (Cook and Barbour, 2015; Long et al., 2019; Moody et al., 1994), and without apparent consequence for fitness (Schwanz et al., 2011; Voordouw et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies examining fitness in infected deermice.

claim: Within 2 hr of LPS treatment, animals of both P. leucopus and M. musculus displayed piloerection and sickness behavior.
source: Within 2 hr LPS-treated animals of both species displayed piloerection and sickness behavior, that is reduced activity, hunched posture, and huddling.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental protocol described in the Results section.

claim: By 4 hr after LPS treatment, 8 of 10 M. musculus had tachypnea, while only one of ten LPS-treated P. leucopus displayed this sign (p=0.005).
source: By the experiment's termination at 4 hr, 8 of 10 M. musculus treated with LPS had tachypnea, while only one of ten LPS-treated P. leucopus displayed this sign of the sepsis state (p=0.005).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis showing a significant difference between species.

claim: Deermice had lower mean hematocrit at 42% compared to M. musculus at 56% (p<0.01).
source: But overall the deermice had lower mean (95% confidence interval) hematocrit at 42 (36-48)%, hemoglobin concentration at 13.8 g/dL (12.1–15.5), and mean corpuscular volume for erythrocytes at 49 fL (47-51) than M. musculus with respective values of 56 (51-62)%, 16.1 g/dL (14.6–17.7), and 60 fL (58-62) (p<0.01).
evidence: This is hematological data from the experiment with statistical significance indicated.

claim: The mean numbers of white blood cells in the LPS groups in both species were lower than those of control groups.
source: In contrast to red blood cells, the mean numbers of white blood cells in the LPS groups in both species were lower than those of control groups (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by hematological data presented in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Under LPS condition, the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio was 0.18 for mice and 0.64 for deermice (p=0.0006).
source: But under the LPS condition. the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio was 0.18 (0.11–0.28) for mice and 0.64 (0.42–0.97) for deermice (p=0.0006).
evidence: This is experimental hematological data with statistical analysis showing a significant difference.

claim: Eosinophil percentages tended to be higher in deermice at a mean 3.4% than mice at 1.2% under either condition (p=0.004).
source: Eosinophil percentages tended to be higher in deermice at a mean 3.4 (2.1–4.7)% than mice at 1.2 (0.5–1.9)% under either condition (p=0.004).
evidence: This is hematological data with statistical significance.

claim: For P. leucopus and M. musculus, the mean fold-changes in gene expression after LPS were 1.32 and 1.30, respectively (p=0.31).
source: For P. leucopus and M. musculus, the mean fold-changes were 1.32 (1.29–1.35) and 1.30 (1.24–1.36), respectively (p=0.31).
evidence: This is RNA-seq data analysis showing no significant difference in overall fold-changes between species.

claim: GO terms for up-regulated genes in P. leucopus featured 'neutrophil degranulation', 'myeloid leukocyte activation', 'leukocyte migration', and 'response to molecule of bacterial origin'.
source: The up-regulated gene profile for P. leucopus featured terms associated with 'neutrophil degranulation', 'myeloid leukocyte activation', 'leukocyte migration', and 'response to molecule of bacterial origin'.
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-seq data as shown in Figure 3.

claim: GO terms 'leukocyte activation' and 'leukocyte migration' were associated with down-regulated DEGs in M. musculus.
source: Indeed, 'leukocyte activation' and 'leukocyte migration' were GO terms for down-regulated DEGs in M. musculus.
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Distinctive GO terms for up-regulated genes in mice included 'response to virus', 'response to interferon-beta', 'response to interferon-gamma', 'response to protozoan', and 'type II interferon signaling'.
source: Distinctive GO terms for up-regulated genes distinguishing mice from deermice were 'response to virus', 'response to interferon-beta', 'response to interferon-gamma', 'response to protozoan', and 'type II interferon signaling'.
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-seq data comparing the two species.

claim: Among the top 100 mouse DEGs, 20 were constituents of GO terms 'response to virus' or 'response to interferon-beta'.
source: Among the 100 mouse DEGs, 20 were constituents of GO terms 'response to virus' or 'response to interferon-beta' and only hree were members of GO term sets 'response to molecule of bacterial origin' or 'response to lipopolysaccharide'.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the top DEGs and their GO term associations.

claim: Among the top 100 deermouse DEGs, only 2 were associated with virus or type 1 interferon GO terms, but 12 were associated with bacterial molecule GO terms.
source: In contrast, among the top 100 deermouse DEGs, there were only 2 associated with the virus or type 1 interferon GO terms, but 12 were associated with either or both of the bacterial molecule GO terms.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the top DEGs and their GO term associations, showing a contrasting pattern to mice.

claim: Low transcription of Nos2 in both controls and LPS-treated P. leucopus was confirmed by RT-qPCR.
source: The present study, which incorporated outbred M. musculus instead of an inbred strain, confirmed the previous finding of differences in Nos2, the gene for inducible nitric oxide synthase, and Arg1, the gene for arginase 1, expression between M. musculus and P. leucopus (Figure 5; Supplementary file 1). Results similar to the RNA-seq findings were obtained with specific RT-qPCR assays for Nos2 and Arg1 transcripts for P. musculus and M. musculus (Table 2; Table 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is confirmed by both RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data presented in multiple figures and tables.

claim: An increase in Arg1 with LPS was observed in P. leucopus in the 12 hr experiment with lower LPS dose.
source: Low transcription of Nos2 in both in controls and LPS-treated P. leucopus and an increase in Arg1 with LPS was also observed in another experiment for present study where the dose of LPS was 1 µg/g body mass instead of 10 µg/g and the interval between injection and assessment was 12 hr instead of 4 hr (Table 3; Table 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from a different experimental condition, confirming the pattern.

claim: In P. leucopus, the Akt1/Akt2 ratio remained >1.0 even among LPS-treated animals.
source: In both species, the Akt1/Akt2 ratio declined in LPS-treated animals, but for P. leucopus the ratio remained >1.0 even among LPS-treated animals, while in the blood of M. musculus the ratio was <1.0 at baseline and declined further in the LPS-treated animals.
evidence: This is based on targeted RNA-seq data showing transcription ratios.

claim: In M. musculus, the Akt1/Akt2 ratio was <1.0 at baseline and declined further in LPS-treated animals.
source: In both species, the Akt1/Akt2 ratio declined in LPS-treated animals, but for P. leucopus the ratio remained >1.0 even among LPS-treated animals, while in the blood of M. musculus the ratio was <1.0 at baseline and declined further in the LPS-treated animals.
evidence: This is based on targeted RNA-seq data showing transcription ratios.

claim: In deermice, the Cd14/Fcgr3 ratio decreased markedly in the LPS-treated group.
source: In the deermice, the ratio in control animals was midway between the two groups of mice but there was a marked decrease in the LPS-treated deermice (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on targeted RNA-seq data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The decrease in Cd14/Fcgr3 ratio in LPS-treated deermice was not associated with a fall in the absolute numbers or percentages of monocytes in the blood.
source: This was not associated with a fall in the absolute numbers or percentages of monocytes in the blood of these animals (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on hematological data from Table 1.

claim: The Nos2/Arg1, Il12/Il10, Akt1/Akt2, and Cd14/Fcgr3 relationships document a disposition toward alternatively activated macrophages and nonclassical monocytes in P. leucopus both before and after exposure to LPS.
source: Taken together, the Nos2/Arg1, Il12/Il10, Akt1/Akt2, and Cd14/Fcgr3 relationships document a disposition toward alternatively activated macrophages and nonclassical monocytes in P. leucopus both before and after exposure to LPS.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on multiple gene expression ratios from RNA-seq data.

claim: The macrophage/monocyte profile in mice contrasts with P. leucopus, showing a predominance of classically activated macrophages and classical monocytes.
source: This contrasts with profiles consistent with a predominance of classically activated macrophages and classical monocytes in mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on gene expression data comparing the two species.

claim: For mice, the Ifng transcript was one of the top ranked DEGs by both fold-change and adjusted p value.
source: For mice the Ifng transcript was one of the top ranked DEGs by both fold-change and adjusted p value by genome-wide RNA-seq (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on genome-wide RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: For P. leucopus, Ifng was far down the list of DEGs, and the comparably ranked DEG instead was Il1b.
source: In contrast, for P. leucopus Ifng was far down the list, and the comparably ranked DEG instead was Il1b.
evidence: This is based on genome-wide RNA-seq analysis results comparing gene rankings.

claim: There was little or no detectable transcription of Ifng in the blood of deermice in which Il1b expression was high.
source: There was little or no detectable transcription of Ifng in the blood of deermice in which Il1b expression was high.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing inverse relationship between Ifng and Il1b in deermice.

claim: There was scant to no transcription of Ifng in the blood of P. leucopus 12 hr after injection of LPS.
source: There was also scant to no transcription of Ifng in the blood of P. leucopus 12 hr after injection of LPS (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on targeted RNA-seq data from the 12 hr experiment.

claim: Both groups of LPS-treated rats had lowered total white blood cells and lower neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratios compared to controls.
source: Both groups of LPS-treated rats had lowered total white blood cells and, like the mice, lower neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratios compared to controls (Table 4; Table 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is hematological data from the rat experiment.

claim: There were elevations of interferon-gamma, interleukin-6, and interleukin-10 proteins from undetectable levels in the blood of LPS-treated rats.
source: There were also elevations of interferon-gamma, interleukin-6, and interleukin-10 proteins from undetectable levels in the blood of the treated rats.
evidence: This is based on multiplex cytokine protein assay data from rat plasma.

claim: By targeted RNA-seq, there were 24 x fold-changes between LPS-treated rats and control rats for Ifng and Nos2 but only ~3 x fold-change for Il1b.
source: By targeted RNA-seq, there were 24 x fold-changes between the LPS-treated rats and control rats for Ifng and Nos2 but only ~3 x fold-change for Il1b (Table 4).
evidence: This is targeted RNA-seq data from the rat experiment.

claim: LPS stimulated expression of ERV sequences in mice and rats.
source: The results confirm previous reports of heightened transcription of ERV sequences in mice or mouse cells after exposure to LPS (Hara et al., 1981; Jongstra and Moroni, 1981; Stoye and Moroni, 1983). Here we add the example of the rat.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data from the current study and citations to prior literature.

claim: Two of the three highest scoring DEGs in rats by FDR p value and fold-change criteria were ERV gag-pol and env transcripts.
source: Our attention was drawn to ERVs by finding in the genome-wide RNA-seq of LPS-treated and control rats. Two of the three highest scoring DEGs by FDR p value and fold-change criteria were a gag-pol transcript (GenBank accession XM_039101019.1) for an ERV polyprotein and an env transcript (XM_039113367) for an envelope (Env) protein that is similar to that of murine leukemia viruses (MLV) (Table 4; Table 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on genome-wide RNA-seq analysis of rat samples.

claim: There were no transcripts for an ERV Env protein annotated as such among the 1154 DEGs identified for P. leucopus.
source: But, there was no transcripts for an ERV Env protein annotated as such among the 1154 DEGs identified for P. leucopus (Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on genome-wide RNA-seq analysis of P. leucopus samples.

claim: Instead of increased expression of ERV Env protein sequences in blood of mice and rats treated with LPS, there was decreased transcription of the homologous ERV env in like-treated P. leucopus.
source: Instead of increased expression of ERV Env protein sequences in blood of mice and rats treated with LPS, there was decreased transcription of the homologous ERV env in like-treated P. leucopus.
evidence: This is based on targeted RNA-seq data comparing ERV transcription across species.

claim: Similarities in the profiles for LPS-treated and B. hermsii-infected deermice included low levels of transcription of Nos2 and Ifng contrasting with high levels for Arg1 and Il1b expression.
source: Similarities in the profiles for the LPS-treated and B. hermsii-infected deermice were as follows: (1) low levels of transcription of Nos2 and Ifng that contrasted with the high levels for Arg1 and Il1b expression in the same animals
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNA-seq data from two different experimental conditions.

claim: Both LPS-treated and B. hermsii-infected deermice maintained the Akt1/Akt2 ratio >1.0.
source: (2) maintenance of the Akt1/Akt2 ratio >1.0 under both conditions
evidence: This is based on targeted RNA-seq data from both experimental conditions.

claim: Both LPS-treated and B. hermsii-infected deermice showed reduction of the Cd14/Fcgr3 ratio.
source: (3) reduction of the Cd14/Fcgr3 ratio
evidence: This is based on targeted RNA-seq data from both experimental conditions.

claim: Both LPS-treated and B. hermsii-infected deermice showed decreased transcription of Cd69.
source: (4) decreased transcription of Cd69
evidence: This is based on targeted RNA-seq data from both experimental conditions.

claim: Both LPS-treated and B. hermsii-infected deermice showed stable, low transcription of ERV env and gag-pol loci with only marginal increases in transcription of ISGs and RIG-I-like receptors.
source: (5) stable, low transcription of ERV env and gag-pol loci with only marginal increases in transcription of ISGs and RIG-I-like receptors.
evidence: This is based on targeted RNA-seq data comparing ERV and ISG transcription in both conditions.

claim: The responses that distinguish deermice are not confined to the singular case of LPS as the elicitor.
source: Thus, the responses that distinguish deermice are not confined to the singular case of LPS as the elicitor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of responses to both LPS and B. hermsii infection.

claim: Nos2 gene knockouts in M. musculus had lower LPS-induced mortality than their wild-type counterparts.
source: Although Nos2 gene knockouts in M. musculus had lower LPS-induced mortality than their wild-type counterparts, the mutants were more susceptible to the protozoan Leishmania major and the facultative intracellular bacterium Listeria monocytogenes (MacMicking et al., 1995; Wei et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on Nos2 knockout mice.

claim: Nos2 knockout mice were more susceptible to Leishmania major and Listeria monocytogenes.
source: Although Nos2 gene knockouts in M. musculus had lower LPS-induced mortality than their wild-type counterparts, the mutants were more susceptible to the protozoan Leishmania major and the facultative intracellular bacterium Listeria monocytogenes (MacMicking et al., 1995; Wei et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: P. yucatanicus is the main reservoir for Leishmania mexicana in Mexico.
source: While there are no known studies of either of these pathogens in P. leucopus, the related species P. yucatanicus is the main reservoir for Leishmania mexicana in Mexico (Chable-Santos et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Compared with M. musculus, which suffer a high fatality rate from experimental infections with L. mexicana, P. yucatanicus infections are commonly asymptomatic.
source: Compared with M. musculus, which suffer a high fatality rate from experimental infections with L. mexicana, P. yucatanicus infections are commonly asymptomatic (Loría-Cervera et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: P. leucopus demonstrated both tolerance of and resistance to the tickborne encephalitis flavivirus Powassan virus in an experimental model.
source: Both tolerance of and resistance to the tickborne encephalitis flavivirus Powassan virus by P. leucopus were demonstrated in an experimental model in which mice, by contrast, were severely affected Mlera et al., 2017.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: P. maniculatus infected with SARS-CoV-2 virus displayed only mild pathology, manifested little if any disability, and recovered within a few days.
source: P. maniculatus has been successfully infected with the SARS-CoV-2 virus by the respiratory route, but the infected animals displayed only mild pathology, manifested little if any disability, and recovered within a few days Fagre et al., 2021; Griffin et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: P. maniculatus is noted for its tolerance of hantavirus, which commonly is fatal for infected humans.
source: Among natural populations and in the laboratory, P. maniculatus is noted for its tolerance of hantavirus, which commonly is fatal for infected humans Botten et al., 2000; Childs et al., 1994.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: P. maniculatus was permissive of infection with monkeypox virus, but the infection was mild and transient.
source: P. maniculatus was permissive of infection with monkeypox virus, but the infection was mild and transient Deschambault et al., 2023.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Naked mole-rat macrophages and blood myeloid cells have low to absent transcription of Nos2 or production of nitric oxide in response to LPS, even in the presence of added interferon-gamma.
source: These include macrophages and blood myeloid cells with low to absent transcription of Nos2 or production of nitric oxide in response to LPS, even in the presence of added interferon-gamma Gorshkova et al., 2023.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on naked mole-rats.

claim: Like P. leucopus and in distinction to M. musculus, naked mole-rats showed an increase in the proportion of neutrophils in the blood 4 hr after intraperitoneal injection of LPS.
source: Like P. leucopus and in distinction to M. musculus, naked mole-rats showed an increase in the proportion of neutrophils in the blood 4 hr after intraperitoneal injection of LPS Hilton et al., 2019.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research comparing species responses.

claim: The hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells of naked mole-rats had a lower type 1 interferon response than mice to a TLR3 agonist.
source: In another comparative study, the hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells of these rodents had a lower type 1 interferon response than mice to a TLR3 agonist Emmrich et al., 2022.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: A natural population of P. leucopus showed >80% prevalence of B. burgdorferi infection and high incidence of re-infections.
source: Our studies of P. leucopus began with a natural population and documented a>80% prevalence of infection and high incidence of re-infections by B. burgdorferi in the area's white-footed deermouse, the most abundant mammal there (Bunikis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a field study.

claim: Most humans who become infected with B. burgdorferi have a definable illness.
source: Subclinical infections in humans occur, but most of those who become infected have a definable illness (Steere et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published clinical research.

claim: The majority of Lyme disease symptoms and signs are attributable to inflammation elicited by B. burgdorferi's presence and not from virulence properties per se.
source: The localized or systemic presence of the microbe is a necessary condition for Lyme disease, but the majority of the symptoms and signs are attributable to inflammation elicited by the organism's presence and not from virulence properties per se or the hijacking of host cells (Coburn et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature on Lyme disease pathogenesis.

claim: Humans are transmission dead-ends for B. burgdorferi and many other zoonotic agents in their life cycles.
source: Since humans are transmission dead-ends for B. burgdorferi and many other zoonotic agents in their life cycles, it is not surprising that human infections are generally more debilitating if not fatal than what adapted natural hosts experience.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of zoonotic disease transmission cycles.

claim: Interferon-gamma is a determinant of Nos2 expression.
source: Interferon-gamma is a determinant of Nos2 expression (Lowenstein et al., 1993; Salkowski et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: There was a tight correlation between the levels of transcription of Ifng and Nos2 for both species and both experimental conditions.
source: The analysis shown in upper left panel of Figure 10 shows a tight correlation between the levels of transcription of Ifng and Nos2 for both species and both experimental conditions (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of RNA-seq data presented in Figure 10.

claim: A significant correlation was observed between the ratios of Nos2 to Arg1 on Ifng to Il1b across all animals.
source: A significant correlation was also observed for the combined set of animals between the ratios of Nos2 to Arg1 on Ifng to Il1b (upper right panel), an indication of co-variation between Ifng expression and macrophage polarization.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The plausible sources of interferon-gamma mRNA in whole blood are T-cells, Natural Killer cells, and Type 1 Innate Lymphoid Cells.
source: The plausible sources of interferon-gamma mRNA in whole blood are T-cells, Natural Killer cells, and Type 1 Innate Lymphoid Cells Quatrini et al., 2017.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Cd69 encodes a C-type lectin protein and an early activation antigen for T-cells, Natural Killer cells, and Type 1 Innate Lymphoid Cells.
source: A DEG for M. musculus by both genome-wide and targeted RNA-seq (Supplementary file 1) was Cd69, which encodes a C-type lectin protein and an early activation antigen for these cells Heinzelmann et al., 2000.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In P. leucopus, transcription of Cd69 occurred in the blood of controls, but it was the same or only marginally different for the LPS-treated animals.
source: In P. leucopus, transcription of Cd69 occurred in the blood of control P. leucopus, but it was the same or only marginally different for the LPS-treated animals (lower left panel).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data presented in Figure 10.

claim: In M. musculus, the baseline transcription of Cd69 was below that of P. leucopus, while in the LPS-treated mice it was many fold higher.
source: In contrast, in M. musculus the baseline transcription of Cd69 was below that of P. leucopus, while in the LPS-treated mice it was many fold higher.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data comparing Cd69 expression between species.

claim: In mice, transcripts for Cd69 correlated tightly with Ifng transcription, but in deermice there was little correlation between Cd69 and Ifng expression.
source: In mice, transcripts for Cd69 correlated tightly with Ifng transcription, but in the deermice there was little correlation between Cd69 and Ifng expression at those low levels (lower right panel).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of RNA-seq data presented in Figure 10.

claim: CD69-positive cells are a source of Ifng in mice.
source: The findings are consistent with CD69-positive cells being a source of Ifng in mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between Cd69 and Ifng transcription in mice.

claim: Tlr4 expression increased ~threefold more in P. leucopus than in M. musculus after LPS.
source: Tlr4 expression increased ~threefold more in P. leucopus than in M. musculus after LPS (Supplementary file 1 )
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from Supplementary file 1.

claim: The magnitude of the decline in expression of Cd14 in deermice was greater than in mice after LPS.
source: but the magnitude of the decline in expression of Cd14 in deermice than mice was even greater.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data comparing Cd14 expression changes.

claim: CD14 is required for LPS-stimulated signaling through surface TLR4.
source: CD14 is required for LPS-stimulated signaling through surface TLR4 Mazgaeen and Gurung, 2020
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Decreased availability of CD14 for TLR4 signaling is a possible explanation for the moderated response to LPS in P. leucopus.
source: and, as such, its decreased availability for this signaling pathway is a possible explanation for the moderated response to LPS in P. leucopus.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed decrease in Cd14 expression and known role of CD14 in LPS signaling.

claim: Five ISGs (Gbp4, Ifit1, Irf7, Isg15, and Oas1a) had higher transcription in all LPS-treated animals, but the magnitude of fold change was less in deermice, ranging from 6–25% of what it was in mice.
source: Five other ISGs (and encoding genes)—guanylate binding protein 4 (Gbp4), interferon-induced protein with tetratricopeptide repeat (Ifit1), interferon regulatory factor 7 (Irf7), ubiquitin-type modifier ISG15 (Isg15), and 2'–5' oligoadenylate synthase 1 A (Oas1a)—had higher transcription in all the LPS-treated animals. But the magnitude of fold change was less in the deermice, ranging from 6–25% of what it was in the LPS group of mice (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data comparing ISG expression between species.

claim: All four cytoplasmic PRRs (Rigi, Ifih1, Dhx58, and Cgas) were upregulated in the blood of LPS-treated mice and deermice, but the magnitude of fold change was less by 50–90% in treated P. leucopus than in M. musculus.
source: All four cytoplasmic PRRs were upregulated in the blood of LPS-treated mice and deermice (Supplementary file 1). But, again, for each of them the magnitude of fold change was less by 50–90% in treated P. leucopus than in M. musculus.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data comparing PRR expression between species.

claim: For most pairs of ISGs and PRRs, there was evidence of covariation across all 40 animals.
source: For most of the pairs there was evidence of covariation across all 40 animals.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of RNA-seq data presented in Figure 11.

claim: Pathways in P. leucopus for PRR signaling and ISG expression functioned similarly to those in M. musculus but differed in magnitude of the changes, being more moderate in the deermice.
source: These findings were evidence that pathways in P. leucopus for PRR signaling and ISG expression functioned similarly to those in M. musculus but differed under these experimental conditions in magnitude of the changes, being more moderate in the deermice.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the RNA-seq data showing similar patterns but different magnitudes.

claim: Endogenous retroviruses are one of the drivers of innate immune responses to a microbe.
source: The activity of these diverse, abundant, and pervasive elements have been recognized as one of the drivers of innate immune responses to a microbe (Hurst and Magiorkinis, 2015; Lima-Junior et al., 2021; Rangel et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In humans, there was heightened transcription of retrotransposons in patients with septic shock.
source: In humans, there was heightened transcription of retrotransposons in patients with septic shock (Mommert et al., 2020), as well as in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from human subjects experimentally injected with LPS (Pisano et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published clinical studies.

claim: Bacteria like Staphylococcus epidermidis that express TLR2 agonists promoted expression of ERVs, which in turn modulated host immune responses.
source: Bacteria like Staphylococcus epidermidis that express TLR2 agonists, such as lipoteichoic acid, promoted expression of ERVs, which in turn modulated host immune responses (Lima-Junior et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: A synthetic analog of a B. burgdorferi lipoprotein activated human monocytic cells and promoted replication of the latent HIV virus in persistently infected cells.
source: A synthetic analog of a B. burgdorferi lipoprotein activated human monocytic cells and promoted replication of the latent HIV virus in cells that were persistently infected (Norgard et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The suppression of ERV transcription in deermice may be attributable to defensive adaptations of Peromyscus to repeated invasions of endogenous retroviruses.
source: This suppression in the deermice may be attributable to defensive adaptations of Peromyscus to repeated invasions of endogenous retroviruses, as Gozashti et al. has proposed for P. maniculatus (Gozashti et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed ERV suppression and cited literature on P. maniculatus.

claim: P. leucopus has an abundance of Long Terminal Repeat retrotransposons, several named for their endogenous retrovirus heritages.
source: Like P. maniculatus, P. leucopus has an abundance of Long Terminal Repeat retrotransposons, several named for their endogenous retrovirus heritages (Long et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior genomic analysis study.

claim: The P. leucopus genome contains genes for KRAB domain zinc finger proteins, including Zfp809 and Zfp997.
source: But a subsequent annotation round identified several genes for KRAB domain zinc finger proteins in P. leucopus, including Zfp809 (XP_006982432), which initiates ERV silencing (Wolf et al., 2015), and Zfp997 (XP_037067826), which suppresses ERV expression (Treger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation data and supported by citations to functional studies of these genes.

claim: P. leucopus has higher baseline expression of some ISGs compared to M. musculus.
source: Another possible adaptation in P. leucopus is the higher baseline expression of some ISGs as noted here (Figure 11; Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing ISG expression in control animals.

claim: The feature that may best distinguish the deermouse from the mouse and rat is its predominantly anti-inflammatory quality.
source: But the feature that may best distinguish the deermouse from the mouse and rat is its predominantly anti-inflammatory quality.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the overall pattern of results from the study.

claim: The anti-inflammatory characteristic of P. leucopus likely has a complex, polygenic basis, with environmental and epigenetic influences.
source: This characteristic likely has a complex, polygenic basis, with environmental (including microbiota) and epigenetic influences.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the genetic and environmental basis of the observed phenotype.

claim: Deermice showed heightened expression of genes for proteases such as Mmp8, enzymes for reactive oxygen species such as NADPH oxidase 1 (Nox1), and facilitators of neutrophil extracellular traps such as PAD4 (Padi4).
source: But deermice showed heightened expression of genes for proteases, such as Mmp8, enzymes for reactive oxygen species, such as NADPH oxidase 1 (Nox1), and facilitators of neutrophil extracellular traps, such as PAD4 (Padi4) (Supplementary file 1 ).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from Supplementary file 1.

claim: Possible mitigators of neutrophil-mediated damage in P. leucopus include secretory leukocyte peptidase inhibitor and superoxide dismutase 2.
source: We had previously identified possible mitigators, such as secretory leuckocyte peptidase inhibitor and superoxide dismutase 2 (Balderrama-Gutierrez et al., 2021). These findings were replicated here.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from both the current and a prior study.

claim: P. leucopus and P. maniculatus are 'immunocompetent' with respect to the microbes they host and with which they may share a long history.
source: P. leucopus and P. maniculatus, are in this sense 'immunocompetent' with respect to the microbes they host and with which they may share a long history (Hoen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Peromyscus species have successfully adjusted to changing landscapes and climate.
source: The abundance of P. leucopus across much of North America (Hall, 1979; Moscarella et al., 2019) and its adaptation to a variety of environments, including urban areas and toxic waste sites (Biser et al., 2004; Levengood and Heske, 2008; Munshi-South and Kharchenko, 2010), indicates successful adjustment to changing landscapes and climate.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to ecological studies.

claim: Peromyscus species are more closely related to hamsters and voles in family Cricetidae than to mice and rats of family Muridae.
source: Peromyscus species, including the hantavirus reservoir P. maniculatus (Morzunov et al., 1998), are more closely related to hamsters and voles in family Cricetidae than to mice and rats of family Muridae (Bradley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.
